Chapter 16.1

What Is the Function of the Human Sexual Reproductive System?

Every person alive began as one cell about the size smaller than a full stop. What had to happen for that cell to exist at all?


Learning Objectives

What you will be able to do by the end

By the end of these slides, you will be able to do the following:

  • State that a fertilised egg is the output of the human sexual reproductive system.
  • Define fertilisation as the fusion of the nuclei of an egg cell and a sperm cell.
  • State that heredity is the passing down of genetic material from one generation to the next during sexual reproduction.
  • Explain why each child inherits a unique combination of genetic material from both parents.

How to do this: Commit to an answer before you read on — tap the option you think is right.

A baby girl is already carrying every single egg she will ever have

Why this matters

Some couples cannot conceive naturally. In-vitro fertilisation (IVF) exists to help couples conceive.
Sex cells from both parents are mixed in a laboratory and the fertilised egg is implanted in the female's body. 

IVF came to Singapore in 1983, and the first IVF baby in Asia is a Singaporean.

Textbook: pp. 74–75
Core concept

Sexual reproduction needs two sex cells

Two sex cells, made by two different reproductive systems, fuse to create one individual person.

Learn
  • Many organisms reproduce sexually.Sexually means two parents are needed, not one. Each parent gives one special cell each. Those two cells fuse together, and the new living thing grows from the joining of these two cells.
  • The two sex cells are an egg cell and a sperm cell.The egg cell comes from the mother. The sperm cell comes from the father.
  • These sex cells are produced by different parts of the male and female reproductive systems.
  • The young are formed when the nuclei of the two sex cells fuse or join together.The nucleus is the control centre inside a cell. It is the two control centres that must join, not just the outsides of the cells touching. Note: Nuclei is the plural form of the word nucleus! :)
Key Facts
  • Sexual reproduction: the young are formed when the nuclei of two sex cells, namely an egg cell and a sperm cell, fuse or join together.
  • Not all living things reproduce sexually. In asexual reproduction only one parent is needed, such as bacteria. Bacteria simply splits in two. Starfish also produces asexually: a piece of the starfish breaks off and grows into a whole new individual! (Lowkey i think this is so cool)
Test

Core concept

Fertilisation is a fusion, not a touch

Fertilisation is the fusion of sex cells: the nuclei of an egg cell and a sperm cell join together.

Tap or click the graphic to enlarge

Learn
  • The fusion of sex cells is called fertilisation.Each parent gives one cell. When those two cells join together, that joining is what we call fertilisation. It is commonly said that this is when "life begins".
  • A fertilised egg develops into an embryo, and then into a new individual.An embryo is the very early stage of the new individual. It is a tiny ball of cells that keeps dividing and slowly takes shape over the months that follow.
  • The new individual contains genetic material (DNA) from both its parents.Genetic material is like a set of instructions for building a body. Half the instructions come from the mother's egg and half from the father's sperm. The DNA is found inside the nucleus of the cells.
Key Facts
  • Fertilisation is the fusion of sex cells — the nuclei of an egg cell and a sperm cell fuse or join together.
  • A sperm cell touching an egg cell is not fertilisation. Nothing has fused yet.

Core concept

Heredity: Instructions passed to the next generation

Heredity is the biological process in which physical and mental traits are passed down to the next generation. 

Learn
  • During reproduction, the genetic material in the sex cells is passed down.The two sex cells carry more than the cell itself. They carry the instructions, and those instructions travel into the new individual.
  • It acts like a set of instructions for the cells to form a specific organism.Think of a recipe. The recipe does not look like the cake, but follow it and you always get that cake.
    Genetic material works the same way for a body.
  • Organisms continue to produce their own kind unless the genetic material is changed in some way.
  • Some disorders are carried in genetic material and can be passed from parent to offspring. 
    For example: Sickle Cell Disease: A blood disorder where red blood cells distort into a rigid, sickle shape, blocking blood flow and oxygen delivery.
Key Facts
  • Heredity is the passing down of genetic material from one generation to the next during sexual reproduction.
  • Heredity passes down traits that are beneficial, undesirable and neutral, not only the useful ones.
  • Inheritable diseases include sickle cell anaemia and cystic fibrosis.
Test

Textbook: pp. 77–78, Figures 16.4–16.5
Core concept

Why you are not a 100% copy of either parent

Inheriting any trait is a random process, so every child receives a unique combination.

Learn
  • Genetic material comes from the mother via an egg and from the father via a sperm, in a unique combination.Unique means one of a kind. Your brother got a set from the same two parents, but not the same exact set as you, so the two of you are not the same.
  • Inheriting any trait is a random process.Random means nobody chooses. It is like shuffling a deck and dealing a hand. Nothing decides in advance which card you get. It is literally a genetic lottery.
  • Children from the same family inherit some traits from their parents, but each child is still a unique individual.
  • Humans carry a lot of genetic information, thus the number of combinations is staggeringly a lot.
Key Facts
  • An offspring can inherit any possible combination of traits from its parents.
  • Different combinations explain both the similarities and the differences between a child and her parents, and between siblings.
Test

Application

When the system needs help: IVF and CRISPR

Technology can now step into a process that used to be entirely out of human hands!

Learn
  • In IVF, sex cells from the parents or donors are mixed together in a laboratory.In vitro means outside a living body. The joining that normally happens inside the mother is helped along in a dish instead.
  • The fertilised egg is then implanted in the female's body, where it develops.
  • CRISPR is a technique that can be used to edit or change genetic material.If genetic material is a set of instructions, CRISPR is a way of rewriting a line of them. Examples of application of CRISPR includes curing sickle-cell disease:
    Which is an inherited blood disease where a mistake in a person's DNA causes their red blood cells to become hard, sticky, and shaped like a crescent moon (or "sickle"). These deformed cells get stuck in blood vessels, blocking oxygen and causing extreme pain.

    Doctors use the CRISPR "scissors" on a patient's own blood stem cells in a lab, and the body can finally produce healthy round blood cells now.
  • A scientist used CRISPR on twin babies hoping to make them resistant to HIV. His action was criticised by the scientific community. Why do you think his actions were criticised?
Key Facts
  • Even in IVF, fertilisation is still the fusion of the nuclei of an egg cell and a sperm cell — only the place has changed.
  • There was insufficient evidence that the DNA change would benefit the twins, and concerns that their normal body functions could be affected. Ethics and consequences must be debated thoroughly.
Test

Synthesis

Let's Practice:

Three main terms we have to understand!

Sexual reproduction

The whole process: young are formed when the nuclei of two sex cells fuse together.

Fertilisation

The single event inside it: the nuclei of an egg cell and a sperm cell fuse or join.

Heredity

The consequence: genetic material is passed from one generation to the next.
